Good morning, everyone, and welcome to our monthly case conference. This month I would like to present a case from our robotic program. Last fall, we admitted a 58-year-old woman for a robotic gallbladder surgery. She had had pain after meals for about a year. On the day of the surgery, we were working on the second port when the robot showed an error message. The arm had stopped, and the screen was blinking. My first assistant had seen this error before, so she restarted the arm in less than two minutes, and we continued. There were no complications. The patient recovered well, and we discharged her the next morning. The lesson for all of us is simple: training the whole team, not only the surgeon, makes the difference when something unexpected happens. Thank you.

Let me start with the patient. Mr. Ribeiro was sixty-seven, and he had had abdominal pain for six months. We admitted him for a robotic colon surgery. Moving on to the operation: the surgeon was working at the console, and I was watching the monitors, when his blood pressure dropped. He had lost more blood than we had expected. While the anesthesiologist was giving fluids, the surgeon closed the vessel, and in fifteen minutes he was stable again. To sum up, it was a serious complication, but our simulation training worked. He recovered quickly, and we discharged him after four days.
